raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old young female from Kathmandu, Nepal, presented to the emergency department of the Institute of Medicine (IOM) with a generalized painful skin rash along with extensive blistering with mucosal involvement for one day (Figures 1-3). She had history of cough, sore throat, and fever few days prior to the appearance of rash for which she had taken azithromycin orally. On the 3rd day of oral medication, she developed rash which was nonpruritic and painless. There was eruption of bumps starting from the trunk and spreading all over the body. Her eyelids and lip were swollen, and this was later associated with blistering and crusting. Around 20% skin detachment of body surface area was involved. The patient was clinically diagnosed as Stevens-Johnson syndrome-toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS-TEN) overlap with tracheobronchitis. To find out the cause of SJS-TEN overlap, azithromycin was stopped. After 2 days of stopping azithromycin, her clinical symptoms did not improve, rather new lesions were seen. Then, the bedside cold agglutination test was done by cooling the blood taken in EDTA vial at 4 C. Before cooling, the blood formed smooth coating of the tube. After incubation at 4 C for 3 minutes, macroscopic hemagglutination was observed as cell clumping in thin film of blood that clinged to the tube (Figure 4). The clumping disappeared when the tube was warmed at 35.8 C and reappeared at 4 C (Figure 5). So, infective cause of SJS-TEN overlap was suspected, the most common cause being Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Blood was sent for the investigation of mycoplasma IgM and IgG antibodies. Also, serial dilutions of the patient's serum were mixed with an equal volume of 0.2% washed human O group erythrocytes, and clumping was observed till titer of 1 : 128 dilution after leaving at 4 C overnight (Figure 6). The clumping is dissociated at 37 C (Figure 7).
The complete blood count revealed total leukocyte count of 8000/mul with lymphocytes of 60% with elevated ESR (70 mm/hour). Her liver enzymes and serum creatinine were normal. Test for syphilis (RPR and TPHA), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B and C viruses, herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus, influenza A/B, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative.
She was restarted with drug azithromycin and added hydrocortisone, paracetamol, betadine gargle, mupirocin, and ciprofloxacin ointment. Punch biopsy of her skin demonstrated subepidermal inflammation with necrotizing infundibular epithelium and necrotic keratinocytes consistent with SJS. Mycoplasma IgM antibody report was positive (2550 U/ml), which suggested the current infection and confirmed our diagnosis. The same treatment was continued and her clinical symptoms improved (Figure 8).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old female from Kathmandu, Nepal, presented with a 1-day history of a generalized painful blistering skin eruption and severe oral/ocular mucosal involvement following a prodrome of cough, sore throat, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Several days prior to presentation, the patient developed cough, sore throat, and fever and took oral azithromycin. On day 3 of azithromycin, she developed a truncal papular eruption that rapidly generalized over 24 hours into painful epidermal blistering and detachment involving ~20% of body surface area alongside severe eyelid and lip swelling, blistering, and hemorrhagic crusting. Discontinuing azithromycin for 2 days failed to halt new blister formation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prodromal fever, cough, sore throat, generalized painful skin blistering/detachment, and ocular/labial mucositis. Recent medication: oral azithromycin.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous and mucosal examination revealed generalized erythematous maculopapular and bullous lesions with epidermal detachment covering approximately 20% of total body surface area, accompanied by severe edematous, blistered, and crusted eyelids and lips (mucositis) and tracheobronchitis.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed WBC 8,000/uL (60% lymphocytes) and elevated ESR (70 mm/h) with normal liver enzymes and creatinine. Bedside cold agglutinin test in an EDTA tube showed reversible macroscopic erythrocyte clumping at 4 C that resolved at 35.8-37 C, with a quantitative cold agglutinin titer of 1:128. Serum Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM antibody was strongly positive at 2,550 U/mL. Tests for syphilis (RPR and TPHA), HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV, EBV, influenza A/B, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy histopathology demonstrated subepidermal bullous inflammation with necrotizing infundibular epithelium and full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte necrosis diagnostic of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed Mycoplasma pneumoniae-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome-toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS-TEN) overlap (20% BSA detachment) with cold agglutinin positivity (titer 1:128) and high-titer Mycoplasma IgM (2,550 U/mL; syphilis and viral etiologies excluded). Azithromycin was safely re-initiated to eradicate Mycoplasma pneumoniae alongside systemic hydrocortisone, paracetamol, povidone-iodine gargles, and topical mupirocin and ciprofloxacin ointments, resulting in complete mucocutaneous healing.
